blocks.value: Companies do not all have the same ownership rules. Some are private companies, while others are public companies. These are legal categories. They do not simply tell us whether a business is famous, large or open to customers.

Imagine This: A group of friends start a company that makes sports shoes. At first, the company is owned by the founders and a few investors they know. Later, the owners consider raising money from a much wider group of investors. The company may look at becoming a public company, but it must meet legal requirements and follow the rules that apply.

In India, a private company has restrictions set by company law. These include limits on how its shares can be transferred and a restriction on inviting the general public to subscribe to its shares. A public company is a different legal category and must follow the rules that apply to public companies. The exact requirements depend on the law and the company's circumstances.

There is another pair of words that is important: listed and unlisted. A company is listed when its securities have been admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange. An unlisted company does not have its securities admitted to trading there. A public company can be unlisted, so public and listed do not mean the same thing.

For example: You may own shares in an unlisted public company. You are a shareholder, but you may not be able to buy or sell those shares as easily as shares traded on a stock exchange. When a company lists its shares, investors can trade them through the exchange, subject to its rules and the market's available buyers and sellers.

A company may choose to list its shares to reach more investors and create a place where those shares can be traded. Listing also brings extra responsibilities, such as sharing important information with the public and following stock-exchange and securities rules. It does not guarantee that the company will do well or that its share price will rise.

Remember these two separate ideas: private or public describes the company's legal category; listed or unlisted describes whether its securities are admitted to trading on a stock exchange. This difference will become important when we learn about IPOs.

blocks.question: What is one feature of a private company under Indian company law?
choices: It can freely invite the public to buy its shares.
It has legal restrictions, including limits related to share transfers and public invitations.
It must be listed on a stock exchange.
It must have only one owner.

blocks.question: What does it mean when a company's shares are listed?
choices: The company appears in a newspaper list.
Its securities have been admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange.
The company has more than 100 employees.
The company is owned by the government.

blocks.question: Can a public company be unlisted?
choices: No, every public company is automatically listed.
Yes, public-company status and stock-exchange listing are different things.
Only if it has no shareholders.
Only if it becomes a private company.

blocks.question: Which statement about shares in a private company is most accurate?
choices: They are freely traded on every stock exchange.
They can never be transferred.
Their transfer is subject to legal and company-specific restrictions.
They always give guaranteed returns.

blocks.question: What can listing provide to investors?
choices: A guarantee that the share price will rise.
A place to trade the listed securities, along with public information and disclosure requirements.
A guarantee that the company will never fail.
A job in the company.
